extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor lawyers, HR professionals, policymakers, and stakeholders involved in FLSA independent-contractor classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Department of Labor's economic reality test under the FLSA to determine whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor, using a multifactor, totality-of-the-circumstances approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional factors (§795.110(b)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory text addresses additional factors but the Department declines to identify particular additional factors in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses the inquiry on whether additional factors are indicative of whether the worker "is in business for themselves or is economically dependent on the potential employer for work." The Department believes this text is sufficiently constrained to narrow considerations while remaining flexible to capture factual considerations outside the enumerated factors. Additional factors may be considered either as separate additional factors or under any enumerated factor to which they are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of independent business organization and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously identified by the Department as a seventh factor it considered in its analysis but not adopted as a standalone factor in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts such as incorporation, business licenses, or receiving an IRS Form 1099 may reflect mere labels rather than economic realities. Such facts may be considered where they actually indicate the worker is in business for themselves, or alternatively under any enumerated factor to which they are relevant. If a potential employer requires incorporation or a license as a condition of work, that may be evidence of employer control rather than independent operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors generally immaterial (mere labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain facts "do not generally indicate whether a worker is economically dependent or in business for themself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department continues to believe that "such facts as the place where work is performed, the absence of a formal employment agreement, . . . whether an alleged independent contractor is licensed by State/local government," and "the time or mode of pay" are generally immaterial in determining existence of an employment relationship because they often reflect mere labels rather than economic realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of actual practice should not be absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed §795.110 of the 2021 IC Rule, which provided that "the actual practice of the parties involved is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractual or other reserved rights should be considered like any other fact under each factor to the extent they indicate economic dependence. The Department rejects a bright-line rule assigning predetermined and immutable weight to reserved rights or actual practice; significance of each fact depends on its relevance to the economic realities and the specific facts of each relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved contractual rights (including right to control) may be probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserved or unexercised contractual rights can, in some cases, be as or more indicative of the economic reality than actual practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department recognize scenarios (e.g., a staffing agency reserving supervision rights) where reserved rights strongly influence worker behavior even if rarely exercised. Such rights may therefore weigh toward employee status in some circumstances—but are one fact among many in the multifactor analysis and do not automatically determine outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances multifactor test; no single factor determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic reality test is a multifactor test in which no one factor or set of factors automatically carries more weight; all relevant factors must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning predetermined, immutable weights (e.g., always elevating core factors over additional factors or always prioritizing actual practice) is inconsistent with the totality-of-the-circumstances approach and with case law. The analysis must be fact-specific and informed by relevance to economic realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual provisions and labels are not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractual language (including agreements stating independent-contractor status), incorporation, or receipt of a Form 1099 may reflect mere labels and are not dispositive of classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts should be examined to determine whether they reflect the economic realities of being in business for oneself. If such labels result from employer-imposed conditions, they may instead be evidence of employer control. The Department emphasizes substance over form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual practice remains relevant but not exclusively determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual practices of the parties are always relevant to the economic reality test and often (but not always) more informative than contractual possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges that in many—if not most—circumstances, actual practice will be more relevant (e.g., where an employer permits declining assignments in contract but disciplines workers who decline). Nonetheless, the rule does not minimize actual practice; it simply avoids a blanket rule that actual practice is always more relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples is illustrative, not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble examples were provided to illustrate how each factor might point toward employee or independent-contractor status in particular scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each example provides two scenarios (one pointing toward employee status and one toward independent contractor status) and is meant as an aid to apply the discussion of each factor. No example attempts to determine ultimate worker status or to substitute for the full totality-of-the-circumstances analysis; additional facts could change the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment factor guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of the investments factor should compare the nature (and sometimes relative sizes) of the worker's and employer's investments to determine whether the worker's investments suggest operating an independent business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the worker's investments further an independent business beyond completing specific jobs for the employer. Relative size matters less than whether the types of investments are similar in nature and indicative of business operation. Examples: minor tools used only on jobs for an employer may point toward employee status; marketing, office space, or equipment that supports an ongoing independent business may point toward independent-contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral (centrality) factor guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral factor examines whether the worker's tasks are core to the functioning of the employer's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core tasks are those the employer "could not function without" (e.g., farmworkers picking tomatoes for a farm). Peripheral tasks (e.g., non-payroll accounting support) that are not essential to daily operations are less likely to indicate employee status. The Department uses a common-sense approach to identify what activities are central or important to the employer's business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and initiative factor guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: This factor looks at the worker's technical skill and evidence of business-like initiative (e.g., marketing), not solely the presence of specialized skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialized technical skills alone should not be conflated with business initiative. Evidence that a worker markets their services or otherwise takes business-like steps to obtain work can be probative of independent-contractor status. Examples should illustrate how marketing or other initiative distinguishes between workers with similar technical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss factor guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunity for profit or loss evaluates whether the worker can realize business gains or suffer losses from managerial decisions (e.g., marketing, investments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active marketing or other business-seeking activity may be probative of being in business for oneself but is not a mandatory requirement—workers who rely on one client can still be independent contractors. Examples are intended to show how particular facts may be probative, not to create rigid requirements.
